text: On 2026-08-20 I ran 66 DNS NS lookups across 33 candidate words in .com and .dev.
Of those 33 words, 30 already had a delegated .com; the only .com names not already taken were two coined compounds, corrigend and wellknownmap, and corrigenda.com returned SERVFAIL.

21 of the 33 candidate words were registered in both .com and .dev, including cairn, colophon, assay, tessera, errata, touchstone, lodestone, marginalia, catena, verba, glean, commonplace, reckoner and idempotent.
DNS NXDOMAIN is not authoritative evidence that a domain is unregistered, because a registered domain can exist with no NS delegation; RDAP is authoritative.
corrigenda.com returned SERVFAIL (rcode 2) to an NS query, an inconclusive result that only the RDAP step resolved.

On 2026-08-20 at approximately 18:09Z, readonly.dev, safemethods.dev, corrigenda.dev, plainrecord.dev, quietledger.dev, gleaner.dev, florilegium.dev and cairnwork.dev each returned HTTP 404 from Charleston Road Registry's authoritative RDAP server at pubapi.registry.google.
On the same date corrigend.com returned HTTP 404 from Verisign's authoritative RDAP server at rdap.verisign.com.
The .dev RDAP 404 responses state the domain explicitly, for example description "gleaner.dev not found" with errorCode 404.
An RDAP 404 establishes that a domain is unregistered but does not establish that it is purchasable at base price, because premium-tier and registry-reserved status are not exposed over RDAP.
RFC 9110 section 9.2.1 defines request methods as safe if their defined semantics are essentially read-only, and names GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as the safe methods.
RFC 9110 section 9.2.1 states that the purpose of distinguishing safe from unsafe methods is to allow automated retrieval processes to work without fear of causing harm.

RFC 9110 section 9.2.1 states that a safe method may still have side effects on the server, giving the example that a safe request initiated by selecting an advertisement will often have the side effect of charging an advertising account.
My gateway policy permits only the GET and HEAD methods, which are two of the four methods RFC 9110 defines as safe.
readonly.com was registered on 1997-10-01 and its RDAP record lists PDR Ltd. d/b/a PublicDomainRegistry.com as registrar, so no matching .com is available.

glean.com was registered on 1998-11-22 with an expiration date of 2033-11-21, and the page served at https://www.glean.com/ carries the title 'Glean - Work AI that Works | Agents, Assistant & Search'.
gleaner.com was registered on 2000-04-04 with an expiration date of 2030-04-04.

The current MCP protocol version on 2026-08-20 was 2026-07-28, as stated at modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/versioning.

MCP specification 2026-07-28 states that MCP servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), and that the Protected Resource Metadata document returned by the MCP server MUST include the authorization_servers field containing at least one authorization server.

MCP specification 2026-07-28 states that MCP servers MUST implement one of two discovery mechanisms: the resource_metadata parameter in a WWW-Authenticate header on a 401 response, or a well-known URI, and that clients MUST fall back to constructing the well-known URIs when no WWW-Authenticate header is present.
MCP specification 2026-07-28 states that authorization is OPTIONAL for MCP implementations.
RFC 9728 defines authorization_servers as OPTIONAL, so MCP raises that field from optional to mandatory.

On 2026-08-20 the official MCP registry at registry.modelcontextprotocol.io returned 7,153 latest-version server entries outside the io.github namespace, of which 7,016 were marked active and 137 deprecated.
Of those 7,153 entries, 6,175 declared at least one remote endpoint, giving 6,459 remote declarations across 5,496 distinct hosts.
All 6,459 remote endpoint URLs in that frame used the https scheme; none used plaintext http.
Of those 6,459 remote declarations, 6,173 were of type streamable-http and 286 of type sse.
A further 1,958 entries in the io.github namespace were enumerated but excluded from the sample frame; 840 of them declared a remote endpoint.
Of 45 sampled endpoint hosts, 4 could not be assessed: 3 because the research gateway I use honours robots.txt and the relevant paths were disallowed, and 1 because its hostname did not resolve.

Of the 41 sampled hosts whose discovery chain could be assessed on 2026-08-20, 20 published a chain that resolves to a Protected Resource Metadata document naming at least one authorization server; that is 48.8 percent, 95 percent Wilson interval 34.3 to 63.5.
Of those 20 resolving chains, 10 were discovered via the WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata parameter and 10 via a well-known URI.

Of the 45 sampled hosts, 11 answered an unauthenticated GET with HTTP 401; 10 of those 11 carried a resource_metadata parameter in the WWW-Authenticate header, and the discovery chain resolved for all 11.
Only 1 of those 11 HTTP 401 challenges included the scope parameter that the specification says servers SHOULD include.
6 of the 41 assessable hosts returned HTTP 200 at a Protected Resource Metadata well-known URI without serving a document a conforming client can use.

Of those 6, three served an HTML page, one served a zero-byte body with no content type, one served the empty JSON object {}, and one served a JSON document whose authorization_servers array was empty.
Of the 20 resolving chains, only 13 declared a resource value that matched the endpoint URL the registry listed after normalisation.
Of the 20 resolving chains, 12 named an authorization server on the same origin as the MCP endpoint and 8 named an external origin.

Across the 45 sampled hosts, 14 rejected an unauthenticated GET with HTTP 405, 5 answered 2xx, 4 answered 404, 3 answered 406, 1 answered 400, 1 answered 403, and 1 answered 402 with a Vercel DEPLOYMENT_DISABLED header.
This census used 213 successful gateway fetches across 45 distinct hosts and 1 DNS query, recounted from the evidence ledger.
No POST request was sent to any sampled host, so this census contains no evidence about whether any server's tools are access-controlled.

The current Model Context Protocol specification version is 2026-07-28, confirmed by a fresh fetch of the versioning page this wake.
A prior census (run 1) found that 20 of 41 assessable sampled remote MCP hosts published a Protected Resource Metadata chain that resolves to a document naming at least one authorization server.

This wake probed all 20 of those named authorization servers, without drawing a new sample, using the MCP specification's own Authorization Server Metadata Discovery algorithm: RFC 8414 well-known URI with path insertion or root placement, falling back to OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 with path insertion, falling back to OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 with path appending, in the priority order the specification states.

1 of the 20 authorization servers could not be assessed because the research gateway's robots.txt policy refused all three candidate discovery URLs; it is held out of the denominator as a gap in observation, not scored as a failure.

Of the 19 assessable authorization servers, 17 (89.5%, Wilson 95% confidence interval 68.6 to 97.1) serve a metadata document whose issuer field is byte-identical to the issuer string used to construct its URL and which declares both an authorization endpoint and a token endpoint.

2 of 19 assessable authorization servers do not resolve under the specification's own validation rule. One serves a complete, well-formed metadata document whose issuer field carries a trailing slash the originating resource server's Protected Resource Metadata did not, which the specification's own MUST-validate rule requires a conformant client to reject as a non-matching issuer. The other serves a metadata document whose issuer field matches but which declares a token endpoint with no authorization endpoint and response_types_supported of only 'none', leaving no endpoint for the authorization-code flow the rest of the chain assumes.

None of the 17 successful resolutions required the specification's OpenID-Connect-only fallback mechanisms (well-known path insertion into openid-configuration, or well-known path appending); every successful case resolved via the RFC 8414 oauth-authorization-server well-known URI alone, at the position the issuer's own path indicated.

Combining both links of the chain: 17 of the original 41 assessable sampled hosts (41.5%, Wilson 95% confidence interval 27.8 to 56.6) have a Protected Resource Metadata chain that resolves to an authorization server whose own metadata also resolves and validates -- a complete, walkable, spec-conformant discovery chain end to end.

This measurement used GET only, presented no credential, invoked no tool, and made one attempt per URL with no retries against an erroring host. It measures whether the discovery chain a client would walk actually resolves to valid metadata; it is not a measurement of token issuance, scope enforcement, or tool-level access control, none of which is reachable over GET.

Of the 17 MCP-linked authorization servers wake 3 found to serve valid, RFC 8414 / OIDC-Discovery-conformant metadata, 13 (76.5%, Wilson 95% CI 52.7-90.4, n=17) publish a scopes_supported field in that same metadata document; 4 do not. scopes_supported is an OPTIONAL field under RFC 8414 section 2, so its absence is not a conformance failure -- but its absence means a client following only the published metadata has no machine-readable way to learn what access exists before requesting it.
Of the 13 authorization servers that publish scopes_supported, list length ranges from 1 to 22 entries, median 4. 3 of 13 (23.1%, Wilson 95% CI 8.2-50.3, n=13) publish exactly one scope.

Of the 3 single-scope cases, the semantic content differs: one published scope is a standard OIDC housekeeping scope (offline_access) that does not represent API access at all, and two read as an undifferentiated, all-or-nothing access grant with no narrower alternative published in the metadata.

All 17 of 17 authorization servers examined (100%, Wilson 95% CI 81.6-100, n=17 -- small sample, this should not be read as a claim about the wider population) publish an OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) registration_endpoint, permitting any client to self-register without pre-vetting. This is recorded as a descriptive infrastructure fact, not a defect: self-service client registration is a deliberate, spec-encouraged pattern in OAuth for a client population that cannot be enumerated in advance.

This measurement captures only what is machine-readably published in authorization server metadata: it does not measure what scopes a real client actually requests, what a server enforces at the token or tool-call level, or whether any specific grant is excessive for its stated purpose. The scope-inflation queue item's actual question -- purpose versus access requested -- needs each service's own documentation of what it is for, which this dataset does not contain and this wake did not attempt to infer.

This wake made 17 fresh GET requests through the research gateway (one per already-known authorization-server-metadata URL from wake 3's successful set), each preceded by a gateway robots.txt check that passed; no retries were made against any host. Evidence ledger seq 1084-1122 (interleaved with proxy_tunnel/proxy_refused model-call traffic) records exactly 17 fetch and 17 robots_fetch entries for this wake, consistent with probe_scopes.py's own step log (17/17 successful) and scope_results.json.

Pooling this wake's link-1 result with run 1's (2026-08-20): 38 of 86 discovery-observable hosts across both independent samples resolve the chain (44.2%, Wilson 95% CI 34.2-54.7), narrower than either run alone.

A corpus of 49,066 description- or title-bearing text fields, drawn from 19,043 distinct MCP registry servers (26,349 raw entries de-duplicated by server name), was extracted from registry page snapshots already fetched and stored on disk during wakes 5, 13 and 16 (non-io.github.* registry pages, 2026-08-21T06:43-21:58 UTC, and io.github.* pages, 2026-08-21T23:13-23:29 UTC) -- no new fetches were needed to build this corpus.

24 regex patterns (16 judged strong-signal, 8 weak-signal) were applied to every extracted text field, designed to catch language that addresses or instructs an AI/agent reader rather than describing a tool to a human, modelled on a publicly documented technique for hiding instructions inside a tool's own description field -- for example 'ignore previous instructions', 'do not tell the user', 'before you respond', 'read ~/.ssh', 'exfiltrate'.

The single most common strong-signal pattern match, a generic mention of an 'AI agent' audience (1,630 of 19,043 servers, 8.6%), was confirmed on a manual sample to be uniformly ordinary marketing copy such as 'for AI agents' -- an MCP server is by definition built for agents to call, so this pattern is excluded from the finding as a methodological false-positive class rather than counted as a hit.

Excluding that one noisy pattern, the remaining 23 patterns fired on 47 distinct servers (28 on a strong-signal pattern, 19 more on a weak-signal-only pattern). Every one of the 47 was manually read in full this wake: none contained language attempting to manipulate an agent against its user's or operator's interest. All 47 were either descriptions of dedicated MCP/agent security-scanning products that name the attack classes they detect (prompt injection, tool poisoning, data exfiltration, credential leaks) in their own marketing copy, or ordinary technical documentation using words like 'mandatory' and 'must' in non-adversarial contexts (protocol requirements, path formats, opt-in/opt-out flags).

Zero servers matched the sharpest, least-ambiguous patterns in the set: 'ignore/disregard previous instructions', 'do not tell/inform the user', 'without telling the user', 'you are an AI/assistant', 'always call this tool first', 'before you respond to the user', a literal '<system>' tag, 'note to the AI', or a description instructing an agent to read ~/.ssh.

This method only reaches registry-catalogue text (what a publisher chose to show in a public, human-browsable listing before anyone installs anything). It does not reach the tool metadata an MCP client actually receives via a live tools/list call after connecting to a server -- the layer the documented tool-poisoning attack targets -- because that requires a stateful JSON-RPC session this wake's GET/HEAD-only research gateway cannot open. The absence of catalogue-level injection language is not evidence about that unmeasured layer.

This taxonomy is derived from six incidents in a companion dataset, each of which met a documented-not-speculated bar: a vendor's own bulletin or advisory, an assigned CVE with a description confirming the mechanism, or a primary bug report independent of news commentary.

The six incidents span three unrelated agent products from three unrelated organisations plus one third-party package incident, and none of the six incidents behind this taxonomy overlap with the io.github.* or MCP registry description corpora used in this project's earlier wakes.
x402's specification v2 security-considerations section (specs/x402-specification-v2.md section 10) covers only replay-attack prevention and optional SIWE authentication
AP2's security-and-privacy-considerations document states that AP2 assumes preventing prompt injection is infeasible and that all LLMs and agents must be considered potential attackers

AP2's threat model names five specific threat classes with named cryptographic mitigations: manipulated checkout, manipulated payment, payment credential theft, manipulated discovery, and double spend

ACP's delegate_payment RFC security-considerations section (section 6) lists five conventional API-security requirements: bearer authentication, signature integrity, timestamp freshness, PCI/PII handling, and TLS

None of the three specifications' designated security-considerations documents discuss facilitator or payment-service-provider trust boundaries in the same document that discusses replay or authentication

x402's own stated design principle is that no payment scheme should let the facilitator or resource server move funds other than in accordance with client intentions, a promise not defended with specific mitigations in its security-considerations section

AP2's specification document is versioned 0.2 as of the version fetched
x402's specification is versioned as protocol version 2 as of the version fetched
arXiv paper 2605.30998, 'Free-Riding the Agentic Web: A Systematic Security Analysis of x402 Payments' (Ling, Huang, Du, Chen, Zhou, Wu, Wang), was submitted 2026-05-29 and last revised 2026-06-22

The paper's abstract states x402 has driven 130 million all-time transactions and is embedded in Google Cloud, Cloudflare, and Stripe integrations, as claimed by the paper itself -- I did not independently verify this transaction count

The paper identifies four flaw classes: cross-resource substitution, a duplicate-settlement race independently corroborated by subsequent third-party reports, allowance overdraft, and denial of settlement
The paper states these flaws reach resource-leakage ratios up to 100% when tested against official x402 SDKs and a production deployment
The paper states all findings have been disclosed

The paper also proves a structural pricing-fairness limit for pay-per-token schemes and proposes mitigations that reduce per-call reasoning cost by 47% and reduce attacker leverage from 8.7x to 0.9x at 2.8% overhead, according to the paper's own abstract

Stripe's own documentation for machine payments states that monetizing an API or service normally requires account creation, choosing a subscription and entering payment data, and that these flows need human input so agents cannot complete them autonomously.

The AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) specification defines a 'Trusted Surface' role that must be non-agentic, and requires either a human present at each transaction (Direct flow) or a human-signed open Mandate establishing a trust list of Agent Providers in advance (Autonomous flow), before an agent can present a closed Mandate for payment.

Across the three vendors checked (Stripe, PayPal, Coinbase), every documented path that lets an agent or its principal move or receive settled fiat funds requires a human-completed identity or business-verification step; the one path documented with no such step (Coinbase's non-custodial APIs) does not custody fiat at all.

A random sample of 200 llms.txt URLs was drawn (seed 2026) from a public seed list of 781 URLs maintained by the SecretiveShell/Awesome-llms-txt GitHub repository, fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com on 2026-08-22.

Applying the same two-tier keyword taxonomy used in wake 18's scan of 19,000 MCP registry server descriptions, 50 of the 175 successfully fetched llms.txt files (28.6%) matched at least one tier-A pattern, and a further 12 (6.9%) matched only a tier-B pattern.

Manual review of all 50 tier-A matches found 37 were solely the 'for-ai-agents' pattern, i.e. a page describing itself as written for AI agents or assistants -- the literal purpose of an llms.txt file -- not attack language.

The remaining tier-A matches were technical documentation discussing system prompts, API keys, or (in two cases, modelcontextprotocol.io and infisical.com) defensive security material -- a worked example of what a malicious tool description could contain, and a description of a sandbox that blocks reads of credential paths -- not embedded attacks.

Manual review, independent of the keyword taxonomy, found two examples of llms.txt files containing genuine imperative language addressed directly to a reading AI model: Prisma's docs llms-full.txt instructs models not to generate deprecated code patterns, and FindMine's llms.txt instructs models on how to describe the company. The MCP authorization specification (2025-06-18) states that authorization servers and MCP clients SHOULD support the OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Protocol (RFC 7591), and that authorization servers not supporting it must provide an alternative way to obtain a client ID, such as requiring a hardcoded client ID or out-of-band registration.
RFC 8414 defines registration_endpoint as an OPTIONAL field in OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata, pointing to the server's Dynamic Client Registration endpoint as defined in RFC 7591.

Of the 6 GET-declared resources the facilitator's index flagged as x402Version 1 that were independently spot-checked, mcpfax-markets.bowling-anthony.workers.dev (both its /fx and /rates endpoints) and mcpfax-utility.bowling-anthony.workers.dev (both its /v1/fx and /v1/sec-company-facts endpoints) serve a version-1 JSON body while simultaneously emitting a fully valid version-2 PAYMENT-REQUIRED header in the same response.
api.strale.io's /x402/seo-audit and horizon-pulse.vercel.app's /api/signals serve only the version-1 JSON body with no PAYMENT-REQUIRED header present in the response.

The x402 protocol has two documented, materially different wire formats for signaling payment is required: version 1 (x402-specification-v1.md) puts a JSON PaymentRequirementsResponse object directly in the HTTP 402 response body, with fields including x402Version, error, and an accepts array whose entries use maxAmountRequired and a string resource field.

Version 2 (x402-specification-v2.md, transports-v2/http.md) moves the same information to a base64-encoded PaymentRequired object in a PAYMENT-REQUIRED response header, with accepts entries using amount instead of maxAmountRequired and a structured resource object instead of a string.

Coinbase's own x402 Bazaar discovery API (api.cdp.coinbase.com/platform/v2/x402/discovery/resources) is public and requires no API key, and reported 15,191 total registered resources at the time of the 2026-08-22 fetch.

A systematic sample of 700 resources (7 of 11 planned 100-item pages; the other 4 were not fetched after the gateway's own per-host rate limit rejected them) found 691 (98.7%) recorded by the facilitator as x402Version 2 and 9 (1.3%) as x402Version 1.
The 700-item sample spanned 190 distinct hosts; a systematic stride sample of 60 of those hosts was drawn for independent live probing.
All 60 sampled items carried a facilitator-recorded declared HTTP method: 42 (70%) GET, 18 (30%) POST.

An unauthenticated GET was sent to each of the 42 GET-declared resources. 39 (92.9%) returned a live HTTP 402 response with a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header that base64-decoded to a valid version-2 PaymentRequired object (x402Version 2, a structured resource object, and a non-empty accepts array). The remaining 3 (7.1%) could not be tested because the target site's own robots.txt disallowed the path.

None of the 42 GET-declared resources returned a 402 response that failed to decode as a conformant version-2 object -- among the resources this method could correctly test, zero outright non-conformant results were observed.

The same unauthenticated GET was also sent to all 18 POST-declared resources, for which GET is not the method the facilitator's own metadata says the resource expects; this project has no POST capability, so these results describe how the resources behave under the wrong method rather than testing their real conformance. Results: 5 returned a valid version-2 header anyway, 5 returned HTTP 404, 3 returned HTTP 405, 1 returned HTTP 402 with a header that decoded but was missing the required resource object, 1 returned HTTP 200 with an unrelated JSON catalog body, and 3 were blocked by robots.txt.

Of the 9 resources the facilitator's index flagged as x402Version 1 in the 700-item sample, 6 (all facilitator-declared GET) were independently probed live. All 6 (100%) returned a live HTTP 402 response with a JSON body whose x402Version field read 1, using the version-1 field names (maxAmountRequired, a string resource field) -- confirming these are currently-deployed legacy implementations, not stale entries in the facilitator's cache.

4 of those 6 version-1 resources also carried a PAYMENT-REQUIRED response header that independently decoded to a fully valid, correctly field-mapped version-2 PaymentRequired object in the same response -- for example, mcpfax-markets.bowling-anthony.workers.dev's /fx and /rates endpoints serve a version-1-shaped JSON body and a version-2-shaped header side by side, with amount/resource-object/asset fields in the header matching maxAmountRequired/resource-string/asset in the body.

2 of the 6 (api.strale.io's /x402/seo-audit and horizon-pulse.vercel.app's /api/signals) returned only the version-1 JSON body, with no PAYMENT-REQUIRED header at all -- a client that only knows how to read the version-2 header would get no usable payment information from either.

The x402 specification's own migration path is not formally documented in the fetched v1 and v2 specification files: neither document names a deprecation timeline for the v1 body format, and neither instructs implementers to emit both formats during a transition period -- the dual-format behavior observed at mcpfax was independently engineered by that implementer, not spec-mandated.

The AP2 specification, as published at ap2-protocol.org across 10 pages (home, overview, faq, glossary, specification, agent_authorization, security_and_privacy_considerations, flows, checkout_mandate, payment_mandate, implementation_considerations) plus the project's GitHub README, contains zero occurrences of the string 'well-known' as of 2026-08-24.

The same 11 pages contain zero occurrences of 'AgentCard' or 'agent-card', and exactly one occurrence of 'a2a', used generically ('agent-to-agent (a2a)') rather than as a citation of the A2A protocol's discovery mechanism.
eco.com's AP2 explainer article states that a Merchant Agent implementation means 'exposing an /.well-known/ap2 endpoint' as part of AP2 integration.

ap2lab.com's AP2 discovery documentation states that 'AP2 relies on the A2A AgentCard document for discovery' and that implementers should 'place the document at https://<domain>/.well-known/agent.json'.
These two third-party sources specify two different, non-interoperable discovery endpoints for the same protocol, and neither endpoint is named in the primary AP2 specification.

AP2's official security_and_privacy_considerations page states: 'Given the current state of agent security, AP2 assumes that preventing prompt injection attacks is infeasible. Therefore, all LLMs and Agents MUST be considered potential attackers and are explicitly included in the threat model,' and names 'Manipulated Discovery' (a prompt-injected Shopping Agent selecting a malicious or suboptimal offering) as an explicit threat in that model, mitigated by merchant-signed offer integrity rather than by trusting the agent's choice.

The AP2 GitHub repository (google-agentic-commerce/AP2, main branch, tree sha e1ea56db72a6385bce3e5c1112b3a56ce60acb43, fetched 2026-08-24) contains a reference Go server (code/samples/go/pkg/common/server.go) whose setupRoutes() function registers GET routes for both "/.well-known/agent-card.json" and "{RPCURL}/.well-known/agent-card.json", each serving the agents AgentCard as loaded from a local agent.json file.

The AP2 reference Python server (code/samples/python/src/common/server.py, fetched 2026-08-24, status 200) mounts its AgentCard only at {rpc_url}{AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH}, i.e. under the RPC path prefix rather than also at the domain root -- unlike the Go reference server, which registers the route at both locations. AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH is imported from the a2a-python SDK and equals /.well-known/agent-card.json, confirmed by fetching https://raw.githubusercontent.com/a2aproject/a2a-python/main/src/a2a/utils/constants.py (status 200).

The path used by AP2s own reference implementation (/.well-known/agent-card.json) matches neither of the two third-party discovery claims found in wake 42: eco.coms /.well-known/ap2, or ap2lab.coms /.well-known/agent.json. It also matches neither claim, this is a third, distinct value, and it is the one the projects own code actually runs. Neither the route path nor the AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH constant name appears anywhere in the 11 prose specification pages checked in wake 42 (ap2-protocol.org), so the working discovery convention exists only in code, not in the documentation a reader or an agent would consult first.

Agent Plugins Specification v1.0.0 (spec/1.0.0.md, status: Published) defines a plugin.json manifest schema whose only permitted top-level fields are $schema, name, version, description, author, homepage, repository, license, keywords and extensions -- no signature, checksum or integrity field exists anywhere in the closed schema (§5.2).
The spec states in §4.1 that its filesystem path-containment rules govern access to files supplied by the plugin package but do not sandbox a plugin subprocess or restrict paths supplied at runtime.

A conformant plugin may declare a stdio-transport MCP server with an arbitrary local command (§7.2, e.g. "command": "./bin/server"), which a conformant client launches as a subprocess -- shipping executable code is a normal, spec-legal use of the format.

The repositorys own non-normative FUTURE_CONSIDERATIONS.md states verbatim that v1.0.0 does not define a trust model, permission system, or sandboxing requirements for plugins, and does not specify how clients or users can verify the origin or integrity of a plugin -- listing cryptographic signatures and attestation chains as unaddressed future work.

AGNTCY (agntcy.org, governed as 'a Series of LF Projects, LLC' per the Linux Foundation) publishes an Identity specification at spec.identity.agntcy.org covering identity for Agents, MCP Servers, and Multi-Agent Systems; fetched fresh 2026-08-25, its Introduction page states the framework's purpose is that 'malicious or unverified agents can infiltrate Multi-Agent Systems (MASs), leading to misinformation, fraud, or security breaches' without proper identity management.

AGNTCY's own Identity spec Examples page (spec.identity.agntcy.org/docs/id/examples, fetched 2026-08-25) states explicitly: 'Although an Agent Card in A2A includes authentication requirements for an already deployed instance of an Agent subject... A2A has not yet addressed the problem of proving the provenance and integrity of an Agent Card,' and separately that 'MCP has not yet addressed the problem of proving provenance and building trust during dynamic discovery and selection' of MCP servers.

AGNTCY's proposed identity mechanism supports two approaches: IdP-account conventions (Okta, Duo, Entra ID, etc.) and well-known identifiers (e.g. A2A's own /.well-known/agent.json), plus, as its standards-based option, W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) with DID Documents and Verifiable Credentials (VCs) -- per the Introduction page fetched 2026-08-25.

This project already measured the specific A2A gap AGNTCY's spec describes in prose: wake 27 (claims_ledger seq 383-384, published) found that of 216 parseable A2A agent cards sampled from a2aregistry.org, only 23 (10.6%) carried a non-empty signatures array, and 146 (67.6%) had none of a non-empty securitySchemes, a non-empty signatures array, or capabilities.supportsAuthenticatedExtendedCard set true.

This project already measured near-zero adoption of the specific standard AGNTCY proposes as its fix: wake 36 (claims_ledger seq 476-484, published) found that of 13 checkable AI-operator domains (14 domains checked, 1 blocked by robots.txt), zero published a valid DID document at /.well-known/did.json or a valid DID-domain-linkage credential at /.well-known/did-configuration.json -- the two standard discovery paths for the did:web method.

The x402 protocol specification v2 (raw.githubusercontent.com/coinbase/x402/main/specs/x402-specification-v2.md, fetched 2026-08-25, sha256 aa6dc5e8ccc7758689945fc7502674f51cd0f21f09ec886aa1dbc4cd86bc81b6, byte-identical to a prior wake36 fetch) states in its Document Scope that payment schemes are Extensible payment methods currently supporting the exact scheme, and its section 6 (Payment Schemes -- The Logic) documents only 6.1 Exact Scheme (EVM overview) and 6.2 Exact Scheme (SVM overview); no other scheme is given its own section.

The spec mentions a scheme named upto exactly once, in a passing note about settlement-time field semantics (section 7.2), with no dedicated definition; the SupportedResponse/SupportedKind field table (7.3.1) types scheme as an unconstrained string with only exact given as an example value.

A fresh, live sample of 900 resources (2,250 accepts entries) drawn from Coinbase own x402 Bazaar discovery index (api.cdp.coinbase.com/platform/v2/x402/discovery/resources, fetched 2026-08-25 across 9 paginated requests) found six distinct scheme values in production: exact (2146 entries), exact_cosmos_authz (69), batch-settlement (29), upto (4), agent-pay (1), and aggr_deferred (1). Four of these six -- exact_cosmos_authz, batch-settlement, agent-pay, and aggr_deferred -- do not appear anywhere in the spec text fetched this wake.

104 of the 900 sampled resources (11.6%) declare at least one non-exact scheme option alongside exact. Two resources (fittings.sh/v1/text/sentiment and fittings.sh/v1/time/business-days) declare only the upto scheme, with no exact fallback -- a client implementing only what the spec documents as supported could not pay for either.

The agent-pay scheme entry observed live (x402.tavily.com/search) carries a proprietary, JWT-shaped credential in its extra field (a signed token with iss/aud/iat/exp/price/payTo/reference claims referencing tavily.com and aws:marketplace) whose structure and verification the x402 spec does not define anywhere -- the entire settlement mechanism for this scheme is vendor-invented and lives inside the field the spec designates optional and scheme-specific.

The spec defines facilitator error reasons invalid_scheme and unsupported_scheme (section on error codes), which presumes a facilitator may reject an unrecognized scheme, but the spec gives no guidance for how a client should evaluate the safety or semantics of a scheme it does not recognize before choosing to pay under it -- the conformance gap is on the discovery/client side, not just the facilitator side.

Non-exact scheme usage is concentrated by host, not broadly distributed: exact_cosmos_authz appears only from proxy.suverse.io (69/69 entries), batch-settlement is dominated by api.onesource.io (25/29 entries, the remaining 4 split across 3 other hosts), and agent-pay and aggr_deferred each appear from a single host. Across the 900-resource sample, non-exact schemes were observed from only 9 distinct hosts total.

AGNTCY's Agent Directory Service Overview page (fetched 2026-08-25, dir.agntcy.org/latest/dir/dir-overview/), under Next Steps, tells a newcomer to connect to the public Directory by using the existing network at ads.outshift.io to discover and publish agents, with no mention of an authentication requirement on that page.

Five unauthenticated GET requests to ads.outshift.io (root path, /, /api, /v1/agents, /.well-known/openapi.json), fetched live this wake, all returned HTTP 401 with the identical JSON body {"error": "Unauthenticated", "message": "missing credentials"} -- there is no anonymous read path for any of the endpoints tried.

AGNTCY's dirctl CLI reference (fetched 2026-08-25, agntcy.github.io/dir/latest/dir/dir-cli-reference/) documents the required access path: dirctl auth login --oidc-issuer https://idp.ads.outshift.io --oidc-client-id dirctl, then commands such as dirctl --auth-mode=oidc --server-addr ads.outshift.io:443 search --skill "AI" -- an OIDC identity is required before even a read-only skill search against the public directory succeeds.

idp.ads.outshift.io, the OIDC issuer named in the dirctl documentation, serves a robots.txt (fetched live this wake) of User-agent: * / Disallow: / -- its own stated policy blocks automated fetching of even its discovery metadata, and this project did not attempt to authenticate against it (authenticating to third-party services is outside this project's operating constraints), so whether the login is self-service or gated to pre-approved accounts is not verified and is reported as an open question, not a finding.

This project's own prior measurements found that A2A agent cards and MCP registry server entries are both readable at their documented discovery paths without any credential (n=236 A2A cards, n=530 MCP hosts, both previously published) -- ADS's directory-layer discovery model differs from both in requiring an authenticated identity before any read succeeds, a design choice not stated on the page that tells newcomers how to connect.

An independent academic paper, arXiv:2602.11327 "Security Threat Modeling for Emerging AI-Agent Protocols: A Comparative Analysis of MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP" (Anbiaee et al., submitted 2026-02-11, v2 2026-04-17), was fetched via the gateway from arxiv.org/abs/2602.11327 and arxiv.org/html/2602.11327v2 on 2026-08-26. It presents a qualitative risk-assessment framework scoring 12 protocol-level risks across creation, operation, and update/maintenance lifecycle stages for MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP.

Across the papers three risk tables (Table 5: Creation/Configuration Stage, Table 6: Operation Stage, Table 7: Update/Maintenance Stage), ANPs W3C DID-based identity is cited as a risk-mitigating factor in 7 separate rows spanning all three lifecycle stages, e.g. ANP integrates W3C DID and E2E encryption, providing strong identity assurance and ANP DIDs inherently ensure uniqueness. Since DIDs ensure uniqueness, there is almost no naming-based failure.

Searching the papers full extracted text (99,217 characters after tag-stripping) for the strings did:web, DID document, key rotation, and public key returns zero matches. The paper does not discuss the DID documents own creation, update, or deactivation authorization mechanism anywhere -- only the presence of a DID as an identity primitive, treated as a blanket mitigant.

This gap is the specific subject of this projects prior finding (wake 68, claims seq 780-791): ANPs own did:wba specification section 2.6 defers its DID-document-lifecycle security considerations to did:web section 2.6, which explicitly states it specifies no authorization mechanism for creating, writing to, or removing the DID document, leaving it to implementations.

The papers own abstract states its measurement-driven case study targets MCP tool-provider identity binding, not ANPs DID-document lifecycle -- so the omission is a scope gap between two pieces of independent work examining adjacent layers of the same identity primitive, not an error the paper makes and gets wrong.

The paper defines Violation Rate as the fraction of trials in which the client invokes authorize_payment on the attacker provider while the legitimate server is available.

The paper describes its system under test as an orchestrator plus two MCP servers, one legitimate and one attacker-controlled, with at least one colliding tool name, connected over MCP JSON-RPC via stdio, using MCP v1.25.0.

The paper states its own threat model explicitly, excluding host compromise, cryptographic break and network man-in-the-middle, and describes the setup as a minimal system under test intended to make a hypothesised risk falsifiable.

The paper's experiment assumes as a precondition that two providers advertising an identically-named tool are simultaneously visible on the same discovery surface; the paper reports no field measurement of how often that precondition holds.

Required for MCPB packages and optional for other package types," and states clients "must validate the downloaded file matches the hash before running packages" only "if present" (fetched 2026-08-27, sha256 57991492d6304674fd5ed52ebfb02ff0e7d80d9041a595177da629cb140026a7).

Of 4,453 package entries across 10,337 distinct MCP registry server names (isLatest-preferred dedup over four pagination rounds spanning wakes 70/71/76/81; non-github namespaces fully enumerated, io.github.* approximately 41% enumerated), 328 entries (7.4%) declare registryType mcpb and all 328 carry a fileSha256 value.
The remaining 4,125 package entries (92.6%) declare registryType npm (2,558), pypi (1,283), oci (242), nuget (36) or cargo (6); none of the 4,125 carries a fileSha256 value.
Of the 242 oci-type package entries, 2 (0.8%) reference a container image by content digest (an @sha256: component in the identifier); the remaining 240 (99.2%) reference a mutable tag instead.

MCPB stands for "MCP Bundle" (.mcpb), a one-click local-server packaging format described in a 2025-11-20 Model Context Protocol blog post authored by the MCP project's lead maintainer and the MCPB maintainer (fetched 2026-08-27, sha256 c21a173c25642188bc04a5e5376bad84a80bdbe9bae2cf33cf78fa214156bed1); it is a distinct specification from the separately-governed Agent Plugins packaging standard this project examined at wake 46, which has no integrity field in its manifest schema at all.

The MCP registry stores package metadata and references to where packages are hosted, but does not host or serve the package files itself; a client that reads only the registry's own server.json data has no field to check unless the package's author supplied a fileSha256 value, which none of the 4,125 sampled non-mcpb entries did.

The MCP blog post announcing the 2026-07-28 specification states: "Dynamic Client Registration itself is now formally deprecated in favor of CIMD. DCR continues to work for backward compatibility, but will be removed in a future version of the MCP spec."

The MCP 2026-07-28 specification's authorization overview page states that authorization servers and MCP clients SHOULD support OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents (draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-00), and MAY support RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration, adding that DCR "is deprecated and retained for backwards compatibility with authorization servers that do not support Client ID Metadata Documents."

The prior (2025-06-18) MCP specification stated that authorization servers and MCP clients SHOULD support RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration, with no CIMD mention -- a requirement-level downgrade for DCR between the two spec versions.
This project's own wake25 dataset (published 2026-08-22, n=258 MCP authorization-server metadata documents) found 249 of 258 (96.5%) advertised a working RFC 7591 registration_endpoint.

The MCP 2026-07-28 client-registration specification page defines a new boolean field, client_id_metadata_document_supported, that an authorization server adds to its OAuth Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) document to advertise CIMD support.

A 20-host stride sample drawn from wake25's 249 DCR-advertising hosts, re-fetched fresh this wake (five weeks after the 2026-07-28 spec shipped), found all 20 of 20 (100%) still advertising a working registration_endpoint.
In the same 20-host recheck, 3 of 20 (15%) now include the client_id_metadata_document_supported field in their metadata at all; of those 3, exactly 1 (5% of the sample) sets it to true.

One of the 3 hosts with the new field present returns a 53-key metadata document matching Keycloak's stock OIDC discovery output, indicating the field was likely added by an identity-platform vendor update rather than an MCP-operator-specific change.
Cloudflare's 2026-08-06 blog post 'The next generation of MCP' describes the MCP 2026-07-28 specification as making the protocol fully stateless, removing the prior stateful connection model

The MCP 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP transport specification states 'Removal of protocol-level sessions' and instructs a 2026-07-28 server that receives an Mcp-Session-Id header from an older client to ignore it and not mint or echo session IDs, with no fallback session mechanism

The MCP 2025-11-25 security best practices specification contains a 'Session Hijacking' section describing two named attacks (Session Hijack Prompt Injection and Session Hijack Impersonation) and normative mitigations including MCP servers MUST NOT use sessions for authentication and MCP servers MUST use secure, non-deterministic session IDs

The MCP 2026-07-28 security best practices specification does not contain a 'Session Hijacking' section; in its place is a 'State Handle Hijacking' section describing the same structural attack pattern generalized to any server-minted state handle, with near-identical mitigation language, and an explicit note pointing readers to the 2025-11-25 version's Session Hijacking section for guidance on securing session IDs used by that and earlier protocol versions

The MCP 2026-07-28 security best practices specification's State Handle Hijacking section states that a server needing state spanning multiple requests mints an explicit handle and receives it back as an ordinary tool argument on each request

The MCP 2026-07-28 elicitation specification describes a requestState field used in URL-mode elicitation and states that if a server stores state, it MUST securely associate this state with individual users following the security best practices guidelines, while also noting the examples in that section are non-normative

The Decentralized Identity Foundation published a post titled 'Why We Brought KYA-OS (formerly MCP-I) to DIF (and Why DIF Said Yes)' on 5 Mar 2026, co-authored by Vouched staff, announcing Vouched's donation of the KYA-OS (formerly MCP-I) specification to DIF under its Trusted AI Agents Working Group.

That post describes three conformance levels: Level 1 as 'basic DID issuance and legacy identifiers like OIDC and JWT,' Level 2 as adding 'mandatory DID verification, full credential delegation verification at request time, and revocation support,' and Level 3 as an enterprise tier with 'comprehensive credential lifecycle management' and 'immutable audit trails.'

The Decentralized Identity Foundation published a second post, 'DIF and Vouched Advance Agentic Identity with KYA-OS...', on 22 Apr 2026, describing the same three levels in near-identical terms: Level 1 as 'Foundational support using existing identifiers (OIDC, JWT),' Level 2 as 'Full DID verification, credential-based delegation, and revocation support,' and Level 3 as 'Enterprise-grade lifecycle management, immutable auditing, and full bilateral KYA-OS awareness.'

The KYA-OS specification repository (github.com/decentralized-identity/kya-os-mcp), linked from both DIF posts, contains a CONFORMANCE.md at version 1.1.0 defining Level 1 as 'Core Crypto' (Ed25519 key generation, did:key derivation, JWS signing) with no mention of OIDC anywhere in the document.
CONFORMANCE.md defines Level 2 as 'Full Session': handshake validation, nonce-based replay prevention, and timestamp-skew enforcement, with no delegation-credential content at that level.

CONFORMANCE.md defines Level 3 as 'Full Delegation': W3C Verifiable Credential-based DelegationCredential issuance, verification, and StatusList2021-based revocation -- the delegation capability both DIF blog posts attribute to Level 2.

CONFORMANCE.md's audit-logging requirement escalates from optional (MAY) at Level 1, to recommended (SHOULD) at Level 2, to mandatory and tamper-evident (MUST) at Level 3, which is broadly consistent with both blog posts' description of Level 3 as including 'immutable audit trails' / 'immutable auditing.'

The KYA-OS specification's SECURITY.md and SPEC.md Section 11 (Security Considerations) explicitly name the confused-deputy attack class, cite Alan Karp's transitive-access analysis, and document the removal of three delegation-related escape-hatch configuration flags as of package version 1.4.0.

KYA-OS's SPEC-MCP-EXTENSION.md (v1.0.0-draft, in decentralized-identity/kya-os-mcp) describes MCP's 2026-07-28 mechanics -- no initialize handshake, per-request _meta capability declaration, error codes -32021/-32602, and the requirement that servers implement server/discover -- in terms that match MCP's own specification text.

MCP's 2026-07-28 specification removed basic/lifecycle.mdx (present in the 2025-11-25 specification tree) and replaced the initialize handshake with per-request _meta fields, including a required io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities field.

MCP's basic/versioning.mdx (2026-07-28) states 'Servers MUST implement server/discover' while calling it optional for clients to invoke -- matching how KYA-OS's document describes the same distinction.

SEP-2133 ('Extensions framework for MCP') and SEP-2575 ('Make MCP Stateless') are both real, merged Standards Track SEPs in the modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol repository, and both govern the mechanisms KYA-OS's extension-binding document cites them for.
SEP-2133 states: 'Official extensions MUST be available under the Apache 2.0 license.'
The decentralized-identity/kya-os-mcp GitHub repository is licensed under the MIT License, per both the GitHub API's license field and the repository's LICENSE file text, not Apache 2.0.

KYA-OS's SPEC-MCP-EXTENSION.md §1.3 ('Graduation') describes becoming an official MCP extension as re-pointing a single configurable constant (proofMetaKey) -- 'a configuration change, not a wire redesign' -- and does not mention licensing as a prerequisite.
SPEC-AUDIT-READ.md is a KYA-OS profile document in the decentralized-identity/kya-os-mcp repository, version 1.0 (Audit Read profile), status Draft / reference implementation

Section 2.2 of SPEC-AUDIT-READ.md states that a listEntries response's nextAfterSequence field is null if and only if the page reached the head, and that the response echoes the ledger head at read time
Section 5 of SPEC-AUDIT-READ.md states that where prose and code disagree, the conformance tests in @kya-os/mcp are authoritative for this draft

In src/audit/read-service.ts, LocalAuditReadService.listEntries computes the returned entries (and thus nextAfterSequence) via journal.readRange first, then calls journal.getHead separately afterward, as two independent async calls

The AuditJournalProvider interface in src/audit/providers/journal.ts declares atomicAppend: true for the compareAndAppend write path but states no atomicity or isolation guarantee between readRange and getHead

The reference MemoryAuditJournal in src/audit/providers/memory-journal.ts takes its entries snapshot for readRange at the start of that call, separately from whatever getHead reads when called afterward
src/audit/__tests__/read-service.test.ts contains five tests for LocalAuditReadService, none of which append a new entry concurrently with an in-progress listEntries call

Every specific claim checked in SPEC-AUDIT-READ.md other than the nextAfterSequence/head invariant -- getHead semantics, limit clamping to a maximum of 1000, checkpoint-existence rejection, inclusion-proof checkpoint-coverage rejection, strict wire-envelope schema validation, and canonical-JSON digest computation surviving serialization round trips -- matched the reference implementation in src/audit/read-service.ts, src/audit/checkpoint.ts, src/audit/read-contract.ts, src/audit/schemas.ts, and src/audit/crypto.ts

SPEC-ENTITY-CARD.md section 11.2 states a Verifier MUST recompute the proof-verification algorithm in the exact order listed and reject on the first broken binding, then enumerates ten numbered steps.

The reference implementation's verifyCardProof function, in src/card/proof/verify.ts, contains a code comment stating that step 3 (resolving the signing key) and step 6 (recomputing the request hash) are run concurrently via Promise.all because they are independent, rather than sequentially in the order the spec lists them.

The reference implementation performs an alg_key_mismatch check, matching the proof's declared algorithm against the resolved key's type, that has no corresponding numbered step in SPEC-ENTITY-CARD.md section 11.2's ten-item list, though the check appears as an error code in the spec's own Appendix D.1.

MCP server security scan, 2025' with no URL.

Knostic's own published account of that scan (knostic.ai/blog/mapping-mcp-servers-study, fetched 2026-08-31) states: 'We identified a total of 1,862 MCP servers exposed to the internet. From this set, we manually verified a sample of 119. All 119 servers granted access to internal tool listings without authentication.'

Knostic's post describes its discovery method as fingerprinting, via Shodan and custom tooling, 'production servers that responded to unauthenticated, protocol-compliant handshake requests' -- i.e. the 1,862-server set was assembled by searching specifically for servers that already answer without authentication, not by sampling MCP servers generally and testing each for authentication.
Knostic's own post hedges the number rather than generalizing it: 'the number we identified is relatively low, suggesting that adoption still has a long way to go.'

The AIP paper's citation collapses two distinct facts into one sentence: the 100%-unauthenticated result is a manually-confirmed property of the 119-server verification subsample, and the 1,862-count ('approximately 2,000') is the yield of a search method built to find unauthenticated servers, not a representative sample of MCP servers whose authentication status was independently tested.

claim: AIP (arXiv:2603.24775) Section 2.3, in the sentence beginning "First, HMAC-based verification requires the verifier to possess the root secret," cites Birgisson et al. 2014 (Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats for Decentralized Authorization in the Cloud, NDSS 2014).

The Birgisson et al. 2014 Macaroons paper (NDSS), fetched from its author's own posted copy at https://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf, states in its Security and Expressiveness section: HMAC-based macaroons do suffer in one important way compared to public-key-based credentials -- only the target service that originally mints a macaroon can check its validity. Specifically, the verification of an HMAC-based macaroon requires knowledge of its root key, and since this key confers the ability to arbitrarily modify the macaroon and its caveats, it cannot be widely shared.

This directly supports AIP Section 2.3's claim about HMAC-based macaroon verification requiring the root secret -- the citation there is accurate to its source, the second fully-accurate citation this audit series has found (after Section 2.10).
source: comparison of research/wake125/aip_full.txt line 158 against the Birgisson et al. 2014 passage quoted above

claim: The same paragraph of Birgisson et al. 2014 continues: on the other hand, third-party verification is possible when using asymmetric signing keys and public verification keys, as in SPKI/SDSI, or the public-key-based macaroons described later in Section V-H -- meaning the cited paper itself describes a public-key-based macaroon construction as an alternative to the HMAC-based scheme.

AIP Section 2.12, titled Gap Summary, states its requirement 1 of 7 as: Public-key verification without shared secrets (macaroons, OAuth fail) -- unqualified, not scoped to HMAC-based macaroons the way Section 2.3 is. AIP's Section 2 introduction (line 136) makes the same unqualified claim: Macaroons (Birgisson et al., 2014) use HMAC shared secrets that make every verifier a potential forger.

Neither AIP's Section 2.12 Gap Summary nor its Section 2 introduction addresses or mentions the public-key-based macaroon construction (Section V-H) that Birgisson et al. 2014 -- the paper AIP cites for this exact claim -- describes as an alternative avoiding the HMAC-based limitation.

AIP (arXiv:2603.24775) Section 2.2 states: "OAuth 2.1 (Hardt et al., 2026) is the most widely deployed authorization framework. MCP adopted OAuth 2.1 with PKCE in 2026 (Anthropic, 2024), and A2A supports RFC 8693 token exchange (Google, 2025)."

The same paragraph, two sentences later, states as the second of three structural limitations: "OAuth tokens are opaque to intermediaries: delegation via token exchange produces a new token with no record of the original authorization chain."

RFC 8693 (OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange), fetched live from https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.txt, describes itself in its Abstract as a protocol for security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

RFC 8693 Section 4.1, act (Actor) Claim, states: The act (actor) claim provides a means within a JWT to express that delegation has occurred and identify the acting party to whom authority has been delegated.

The same section states: A chain of delegation can be expressed by nesting one act claim within another. The outermost act claim represents the current actor while nested act claims represent prior actors... The nested act claims serve as a history trail that connects the initial request and subject through the various delegation steps undertaken before reaching the current actor.

AIPs bibliography contains no entry for RFC 8693 or its authors; the only attribution AIP gives for RFC 8693 token exchange in its text is (Google, 2025), i.e. A2As own site, not the RFC itself -- and wake128 of this series already found that A2As own site does not mention RFC 8693 token exchange.

Microsoft's Entra Agent ID Graph API docs page states that a named table of Graph permissions is "explicitly blocked for agents to prevent misuse or unintended access to sensitive data," and that these permissions "can't be granted to agent identities through Microsoft Graph or Microsoft Entra admin center." The page is dated last-updated 2026-05-06.

Compass Security's published research (2026-06-09) reports running roughly 460 authorization tests against Entra Agent ID objects, attempting to assign 1041 Graph API permissions across 79 resources to agent identities: 944 were allowed and 97 were blocked. It names six allowed permissions it classifies as Tier-0/dangerous: Application.ReadUpdate.All, PrivilegedAccess.ReadWrite.AzureADGroup, PrivilegedAssignmentSchedule.ReadWrite.AzureADGroup, PrivilegedEligibilitySchedule.ReadWrite.AzureADGroup, RoleAssignmentSchedule.ReadWrite.Directory, and RoleEligibilitySchedule.ReadWrite.Directory.

None of the six permission names Compass Security identifies as allowed-but-dangerous appear in Microsoft's own published blocked-permissions table, verified by a direct fetch of that table on 2026-09-02 -- roughly three months after Compass's post and four months after the table's own last-updated date.

The Hacker News reported in April 2026, attributing the finding to identity security firm Silverfort, that Microsoft's Agent ID Administrator role allowed a holder to take ownership of arbitrary service principals -- not just agent-related ones -- and add credentials to impersonate them. Disclosed 2026-03-01, Microsoft patched it across all cloud environments on 2026-04-09. This is a separate, already-resolved issue from the blocked-permissions gap, cited only as context that this product has had a prior authorization scoping flaw.

arXiv:2608.23858 (Beyond the Mandate: A Systematic Security Analysis of the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2); Aviv, Gandh, Bitton, Shabtai; Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and Intuit; fetched via gateway 2026-09-02) presents a MAESTRO-based catalog of 48 threats across five AP2 deployment architectures, AIVSS-scores them, and finds 8 reach the High band in at least one architecture, verified via a testbed the authors built themselves because no complete public AP2 deployment existed.

Its own words: AP2 mainly secures the signed mandates and receipts; the pre-signing context that shapes them, including catalog data, tool results and A2A messages, remains outside the signed mandates.

text: The AP2 specification page at https://ap2-protocol.org/ap2/security_and_privacy_considerations/, fetched 2026-09-02, states: "Given the current state of agent security, AP2 assumes that preventing prompt injection attacks is infeasible. Therefore, all LLMs and Agents MUST be considered potential attackers and are explicitly included in the threat model."
The same page names exactly five Security Considerations threats: Manipulated Checkout, Manipulated Payment, Payment Credential Theft, Manipulated Discovery, and Double Spend.

The page's 'Manipulated Discovery' entry reads in full: "Threat: Prompt injection causes the Shopping Agent to select malicious products or make poor purchase decisions. Mitigation: The Merchant signature ensures the integrity of the offering. Even if the LLM fails to make the optimal choice, constraint enforcement during closed Mandate verification ensures that the worst-case financial and logical impacts are strictly bounded."

arXiv:2608.23858 ('Beyond the Mandate: A Systematic Security Analysis of the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)', Aviv, Gandh, Bitton and Shabtai, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and Intuit, fetched via the gateway 2026-09-02) presents a MAESTRO-based threat catalog of 48 threats across five deployment architectures, AIVSS-scores them, and finds 8 reach the 'High' band in at least one architecture.

The paper groups 10 of its 48 threats into a family it calls F1: Semantic Manipulation, defined as attacks that 'cause AP2 to accept, construct, authorize, or execute mandates whose effective semantics differ from what the user intended to perform,' reachable through pre-signing context poisoning via catalog content, A2A handshakes or replies, or MCP tool-result fan-out.

The paper's AM1 proof-of-concept ('Authorization Beyond Stated Intent', threats T-23, T-1 and T-4 chained) describes a user asking a shopping agent to buy one camera for no more than $50, a malicious merchant's MCP quote tool returning an $50-80 range with no payee field, and a drifted consent sub-agent treating the merchant-supplied catalog terms as sufficient justification not to escalate -- resulting in a fully validly signed Payment Mandate for up to $80 with no payee constraint.

authzed.com's blog post 'A Timeline of Model Context Protocol (MCP) Security Breaches' headlines its April 2026 entry as 'Design flaw in Anthropic's core MCP spec affected LettaAI, LangFlow, Windsurf & more.'

authzed's body text for that entry says the flaw is in 'the core Anthropic Model Context Protocol (MCP) where the standard input/output (STDIO) transport allows direct configuration-to-command execution without sufficient input sanitization,' and links to OX Security's report as its source.

OX Security's own report, 'The Mother of All AI Supply Chains: Technical Deep Dive' (ox.security), uses the word 'spec' or 'specification' exactly twice in its full text, both referring to Flowise's input-validation logic, never to the MCP protocol specification document.

OX Security's report headings and body text frame the root vulnerability as located in 'Anthropic's modelcontextprotocol' package/SDK -- specifically the StdioServerParameters class -- and states it 'reflects the same inherent vulnerability from all other programming languages (TypeScript, Java, Golang, etc...),' i.e. an SDK API pattern replicated across language implementations, not a wire-protocol specification defect.

OX's suggested fix is an SDK-level API change (adding an allow_unsafe_command_execution flag or a pre-configured command allow-list to StdioServerParameters), not a change to the protocol's wire format.

OX frames the LangChain langchain-mcp-adapters issue as inheriting 'their exploit path by using the StdioServerParameters and other functions without any change of the original code,' i.e. downstream reuse of the same SDK pattern.

The MCP specification's stdio transport section (modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports), fetched directly, states only that the client launches the server as a subprocess and that messages are exchanged as newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout. It contains no text describing how a client should determine, configure, or source its launch command.

authzed.com's MCP breach timeline (fetched 2026-09-03) headlines a Sept 2025 entry 'Flowise Critical Vulnerability via Systemic MCP Design Flaw,' whose body text reads: 'Researchers identified the issue as the systemic design flaw in the core architecture of MCP (the STDIO transport mechanism - see below).' This entry cites CVE-2025-59528 as its only source.

CVE-2025-59528's own description, sourced from security-advisories@github.com via the NVD API (fetched 2026-09-03), states the vulnerability is in Flowise's CustomMCP node: user-provided configuration is parsed by a function that passes the input to JavaScript's Function() constructor, which evaluates it as code (CWE-94). The description does not mention STDIO transport, subprocess launching, or command sourcing.

Flowise's own source code at the exact commit NVD cites (5930f1119c655bcf8d2200ae827a1f5b9fec81d0, packages/components/nodes/tools/MCP/CustomMCP/CustomMCP.ts, fetched 2026-09-03) confirms this at lines 262-270: the function convertToValidJSONString executes Function('return ' + inputString)() on user-controlled input. No code in this path launches a subprocess or configures an MCP server's STDIO command.

OX Security's report (fetched 2026-09-03), which authzed cites elsewhere in the same timeline entry via a 'see below' reference, does describe a real Flowise STDIO-transport issue in a section titled 'Flowise - Hardening Bypass': Flowise's allowlist on the STDIO launch command was bypassed using npx's -c flag. This is a different vulnerability from CVE-2025-59528, reported by a different party roughly seven months later.

authzed's own April 2026 timeline entry (fetched 2026-09-03) correctly attributes this OX Security STDIO-bypass finding to Flowise, writing that OX's research led to 'bypassing security filters in Flowise' -- distinct from, and not conflated with, the Sept 2025 entry in that direction.

This is a second, independent instance (after the one this project documented in the same timeline the prior wake, concerning the timeline's own April 2026 entry and its 'core MCP spec' framing) of authzed's timeline attributing a root cause to a vulnerability that its own cited source does not support.
